segments.narration: Fifty tons of living red cells rained from the sky. In 2001, crimson downpours battered Kerala, India, staining clothes and stripping trees.
Under microscopes, the rainwater contained no sand or fallout. It was packed with millions of cellular organisms that looked disturbingly like human blood.
Could living microbes actually thrive inside storm clouds? Some researchers even claimed the cells had no DNA, suggesting an extraterrestrial origin.
DNA analysis finally cracked the case. The crimson particles were spores from Trentepohlia, a common tree-dwelling microalgae known to form brilliant red blooms.
The alien theory was dead. But with no tornadoes recorded, how did fifty tons of tree algae launch into the upper atmosphere?

verdicts.claim: Red-colored rain fell across Kerala, India during the summer of 2001.
verdicts.note: The text confirms red-coloured rain fell sporadically across Kerala from 25 July to 23 September 2001.

verdicts.claim: Scientists estimated roughly 50 metric tons of red particles fell in the Kerala rain.
verdicts.note: The reference explicitly states an estimated 50,000 kilograms (50 metric tons) of red particles fell on Kerala.

verdicts.claim: Microscopic examination showed the Kerala rainwater was full of biological cells rather than dust or sand.
verdicts.note: Microscopy revealed the particles were biological algal spores rather than desert sand, volcanic dust, or meteoric debris.

verdicts.claim: Some researchers initially proposed the cells lacked DNA and originated from a meteor.
verdicts.note: The text discusses the panspermia hypothesis proposing a cometary origin, but does not mention any claim that the cells lacked DNA.

verdicts.claim: DNA testing confirmed the red cells were spores from the microalga genus Trentepohlia.
verdicts.note: The reference notes scientists confirmed the presence of DNA and identified the spores as belonging to the green alga genus Trentepohlia.

verdicts.claim: No tornadoes or severe atmospheric updrafts were recorded in Kerala to explain how the spores were lifted into storm clouds.
verdicts.note: While the text notes that scientists found no satisfactory explanation for the uptake and dispersal of spores into clouds, it does not mention tornadoes.
